text: MARITIME COMMUNICATION PROCEDURES Document ID: COM-001 Title: Vessel Communication Procedures 1. GENERAL COMMUNICATION Clear and timely communication is essential for safe vessel operations. Operational instructions should be communicated using clear and unambiguous language. Important instructions should be acknowledged by the receiving person. 2. BRIDGE TO ENGINE ROOM The bridge and engine room should maintain effective communication during maneuvering, departure, arrival and other operations requiring coordination. Changes to propulsion requirements should be communicated clearly. The engine room should report significant machinery problems to the bridge. 3. EMERGENCY COMMUNICATION During an emergency, communication should prioritize information that affects personnel safety, vessel safety and environmental protection. The following information may be important: - Nature of the emergency - Location - Immediate danger - Personnel involved - Actions already taken - Assistance required 4. COMMUNICATION WITH CREW The responsible officer should ensure that crew members understand important safety instructions. Instructions involving hazardous operations should be communicated before the operation begins. 5. RADIO COMMUNICATION Radio communications should follow applicable maritime communication procedures and the vessel's approved communication plan. Emergency and safety communications should be kept clear and concise. 6. COMMUNICATION DURING MANEUVERING During maneuvering, commands should be clear and should be acknowledged when required. The bridge team should ensure that critical information is understood by the person responsible for carrying out the command. 7. LOSS OF COMMUNICATION If communication with a critical station is lost, the responsible officer should take appropriate action according to the vessel's procedures. Alternative communication methods should be used when available. 8. DOCUMENTATION Important operational communications and significant events should be recorded when required by vessel procedures. 9. COMMUNICATION PRINCIPLE When safety-critical information is communicated, the sender should confirm that the receiver has understood the instruction.

CREW OPERATIONS AND WATCHKEEPING Document ID: CRW-001 Title: Crew Duties and Watchkeeping 1. CREW RESPONSIBILITIES Crew members should understand their assigned duties and responsibilities. Personnel should follow instructions from authorized officers. Safety responsibilities apply to all crew members regardless of rank. 2. WATCHKEEPING Watchkeepers should remain alert and capable of performing their assigned duties. A person assigned to a safety-critical watch should not perform activities that interfere with effective watchkeeping. 3. BRIDGE WATCH The officer of the watch should monitor the vessel's navigation, position, course, speed and surrounding traffic. The officer should maintain an effective lookout. Important navigation changes should be communicated to the captain when required. 4. ENGINE ROOM WATCH Engineering watchkeepers should monitor machinery and systems according to their assigned responsibilities. Abnormal temperatures, pressures, sounds, vibration or other conditions should be reported. 5. WATCH HANDOVER A proper handover should occur between outgoing and incoming watchkeepers. Important information should be communicated, including: - Current vessel condition - Machinery status - Navigation condition - Weather - Ongoing operations - Equipment defects - Special instructions 6. FATIGUE Crew members should follow applicable rest requirements. Fatigue can reduce attention, decision-making and reaction time. Personnel should report when fatigue may prevent them from safely performing assigned duties. 7. DRILLS AND TRAINING Crew members should participate in required safety drills and training. Drills help personnel understand emergency responsibilities and communication procedures. 8. EMERGENCY DUTIES Each crew member should understand their emergency station and assigned responsibilities according to the vessel's muster list. 9. PERSONAL CONDUCT Crew members should maintain professional behavior and follow vessel safety requirements. Unsafe behavior should be reported to the appropriate officer. 10. CREW COMMUNICATION Crew members should communicate safety-critical information promptly. If an instruction is unclear, the crew member should request clarification rather than make an unsafe assumption. 11. CREW OPERATIONS PRINCIPLE Effective teamwork, communication, adequate rest and clear responsibilities are essential for safe vessel operations.

Emergency Response Procedure In an emergency, the captain should first assess the immediate risk to personnel and vessel safety. The emergency alarm should be activated when required. The bridge team should maintain communication with the engine room. The chief engineer must be informed about engine-related emergencies. All major emergency actions must be documented in the vessel log.

Engine Room Temperature Procedure The normal engine room operating temperature should remain between 18°C and 35°C. If the engine room temperature exceeds 35°C, the duty engineer must investigate the cause. If the temperature reaches 40°C, reduce engine load when operationally safe and activate additional ventilation. If the temperature reaches 45°C or higher, treat the situation as an emergency and notify the chief engineer immediately. All temperature incidents must be recorded in the engine room log.

FIRE EMERGENCY PROCEDURES Document ID: FIR-001 Title: Fire Detection and Emergency Response 1. FIRE DETECTION Any crew member who discovers smoke, flames or signs of fire should immediately raise the alarm according to the vessel's emergency procedure. The location and apparent nature of the fire should be communicated to the responsible officer. 2. GENERAL RESPONSE When a fire is discovered, personnel should prioritize the safety of people and follow the vessel's emergency response plan. The fire alarm should be activated when required. The bridge should be informed of the situation. The emergency team should respond according to the vessel's muster and fire-fighting plan. 3. FIRE LOCATION The fire location should be identified as accurately as possible. The crew should determine whether the fire is located in: - Accommodation - Engine room - Galley - Cargo area - Electrical equipment area - Deck area 4. ENGINE ROOM FIRE If a fire occurs in the engine room, the emergency response should follow the vessel's approved engine-room fire procedure. The bridge, engine room personnel and emergency team should coordinate their actions. Fuel sources and ventilation may need to be controlled according to the vessel's approved procedure. Fixed fire-extinguishing systems should only be operated according to the vessel's approved system instructions and emergency plan. 5. GALLEY FIRE Cooking equipment can create a significant fire risk. If a galley fire occurs, the responsible crew member should raise the alarm and follow the approved galley fire procedure. Appropriate fire-fighting equipment should be used for the type of fire. 6. ELECTRICAL FIRE Electrical fires require appropriate procedures. Personnel should avoid using unsuitable extinguishing agents on energized electrical equipment. Electrical equipment should be isolated when this can be done safely and according to approved procedures. 7. MUSTER Crew members should proceed to their assigned muster stations when the alarm requires evacuation or muster. Personnel should follow the vessel's muster list and instructions from the responsible officers. 8. FIRE CONTROL Fire-fighting teams should use appropriate protective equipment and follow the vessel's fire-fighting plan. The spread of fire and smoke should be monitored. 9. AFTER THE FIRE The area should be monitored for re-ignition. Damage should be assessed after the situation is safe. The incident should be reported and documented according to vessel procedures. 10. SAFETY PRINCIPLE No crew member should take unnecessary personal risk while responding to a fire. The vessel's approved emergency plan takes priority over generic guidance.

FUEL MANAGEMENT PROCEDURES Document ID: FUE-001 Title: Fuel Monitoring and Management 1. FUEL MONITORING Fuel quantities should be monitored regularly during vessel operations. The engineering team should maintain accurate fuel records. Important fuel information may include: - Fuel type - Tank level - Consumption - Remaining quantity - Transfer operations - Bunkering information 2. FUEL CONSUMPTION Fuel consumption should be monitored against expected operating conditions. Unexpected increases in fuel consumption should be investigated. Possible causes may include changes in engine load, weather, operating conditions or equipment problems. 3. FUEL TRANSFER Fuel transfer operations should follow the vessel's approved fuel transfer procedures. Before transfer begins, relevant personnel should confirm the transfer plan and communication arrangements. Fuel transfer equipment should be checked before operation. 4. BUNKERING Bunkering should be conducted according to the vessel's approved bunkering procedure. Before bunkering, responsible personnel should confirm: - Correct fuel type - Required quantity - Tank capacity - Communication arrangements - Spill prevention measures - Emergency shutdown arrangements 5. SPILL PREVENTION Appropriate spill prevention equipment should be prepared before fuel transfer. Any fuel spill should be reported and handled according to the vessel's pollution prevention and emergency procedures. 6. TANK LEVELS Fuel tanks should not be filled beyond their approved safe capacity. Tank levels should be monitored throughout fuel transfer operations. 7. FUEL QUALITY Fuel quality information should be documented when required. Fuel samples and relevant bunker documentation should be handled according to vessel procedures. 8. LOW FUEL CONDITION If available fuel becomes insufficient for planned operations, the responsible officers should be informed. The captain and engineering team should evaluate the remaining fuel, expected consumption and voyage requirements. 9. FUEL RECORDS Fuel transfers and consumption should be recorded accurately. Records should be maintained according to applicable vessel procedures and regulations. 10. FUEL MANAGEMENT PRINCIPLE Fuel management should prioritize safe operation, accurate monitoring, pollution prevention and reliable voyage planning.

VESSEL MAINTENANCE PROCEDURES Document ID: MNT-001 Title: Machinery and Equipment Maintenance 1. MAINTENANCE PLANNING Vessel equipment should be maintained according to the approved maintenance schedule. Maintenance activities should be planned based on equipment condition, operating requirements and manufacturer instructions. 2. PRE-MAINTENANCE SAFETY Before maintenance begins, personnel should identify hazards associated with the task. Where required, machinery should be stopped, isolated and secured. Energy sources should be controlled according to the vessel's lockout and isolation procedures. 3. AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL Only appropriately trained and authorized personnel should perform specialized maintenance tasks. Personnel should use appropriate PPE. 4. MACHINERY INSPECTION Machinery should be inspected for signs of: - Excessive vibration - Unusual noise - Leakage - Overheating - Abnormal pressure - Abnormal temperature - Damage Abnormal conditions should be reported to the responsible engineer or officer. 5. ENGINE ROOM MAINTENANCE Engine-room maintenance should be coordinated with the responsible engineering personnel. Maintenance that affects propulsion, steering, electrical power or other critical systems should be properly planned and communicated to the bridge. 6. ELECTRICAL MAINTENANCE Electrical maintenance should be performed only by appropriately qualified personnel. Electrical systems should be isolated when required. 7. TOOLS AND EQUIPMENT Tools should be inspected before use. Damaged tools should not be used. Tools and spare parts should be stored safely after maintenance. 8. POST-MAINTENANCE CHECK After maintenance, the responsible personnel should verify that the equipment has been correctly reassembled. Protective devices should be restored. The equipment should be tested according to the approved procedure. 9. MAINTENANCE RECORDS Completed maintenance activities should be documented. Records may include: - Equipment identification - Date - Work performed - Parts replaced - Personnel involved - Test results - Outstanding defects 10. DEFECT REPORTING Equipment defects that could affect vessel safety should be reported promptly. Critical equipment should not be returned to service until it is safe and authorized according to vessel procedures. 11. MAINTENANCE PRINCIPLE Maintenance should preserve equipment reliability while protecting personnel and vessel safety.

Navigation Watch Procedure The officer of the watch must continuously monitor the vessel's position, course and speed. Radar and electronic navigation systems should be cross-checked with visual observations whenever possible. Any significant deviation from the planned route must be investigated. The captain should be informed when navigation conditions become unsafe or visibility deteriorates significantly.

GENERAL MARITIME SAFETY PROCEDURES Document ID: SAF-001 Title: General Vessel Safety Procedures 1. PERSONAL PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT Crew members must use appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) when performing work onboard. Typical PPE includes: - Safety helmet - Safety footwear - Protective gloves - Eye protection - Hearing protection where required - Appropriate protective clothing The required PPE depends on the task and the hazards present.

MARITIME WEATHER PROCEDURES Document ID: WEA-001 Title: Weather Monitoring and Heavy Weather Operations 1. WEATHER MONITORING The bridge team should continuously monitor weather conditions that may affect navigation and vessel safety. Relevant information may include: - Wind speed - Wind direction - Wave conditions - Visibility - Precipitation - Atmospheric pressure - Storm warnings 2. WEATHER FORECASTS The responsible officer should review available weather forecasts during voyage planning and when significant weather changes are expected. Weather information should be obtained from appropriate and authorized sources. 3. REDUCED VISIBILITY When visibility deteriorates, the bridge team should follow the vessel's approved restricted-visibility procedures. Navigation equipment should be monitored carefully. The appropriate lookout and navigation arrangements should be maintained. 4. HEAVY WEATHER When heavy weather is expected, the captain should consider appropriate preparations based on the vessel's approved procedures. Possible preparations include: - Securing loose equipment - Checking deck access - Reviewing the planned route - Monitoring vessel stability - Checking weather updates - Informing relevant crew members 5. STRONG WINDS Strong winds may affect vessel handling and maneuverability. The bridge team should consider wind effects during navigation, maneuvering and port operations. 6. HIGH WAVES High waves can increase vessel motions and may create risks to personnel and equipment. Crew members should avoid unnecessary exposure to hazardous deck areas during severe conditions. 7. STORM CONDITIONS If severe weather threatens vessel safety, the captain should evaluate available options according to the vessel's approved procedures. These may include changing course, reducing speed or seeking shelter when appropriate. 8. WEATHER REPORTING Significant weather conditions affecting the vessel should be communicated to relevant personnel. Important weather-related decisions should be recorded when required. 9. WEATHER PRINCIPLE Weather information should be continuously evaluated because conditions can change during a voyage. The captain should use current, reliable weather information when making operational decisions.
